title: Manila Electric Company v. Benamira
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between legitimate job contracting and labor-only contracting. Where the contractor merely supplies workers without substantial capital or investment and the workers perform activities directly related to the principal's business, a labor-only contracting arrangement exists.
doctrine: Labor-only contracting exists when: (1) the contractor does not have substantial capital or investment to actually perform the job; and (2) the workers recruited are performing activities directly related to the main business of the principal. In such cases, the principal is deemed the direct employer of the workers.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The core issue is whether the arrangement between MERALCO and the contractor constitutes labor-only contracting, making MERALCO the direct employer of the workers.

Article 106 of the Labor Code defines labor-only contracting as an arrangement where the person supplying workers does not have substantial capital or investment in the form of tools, equipment, machineries, work premises, among others, and the workers recruited are performing activities which are directly related to the principal business of the employer.

In labor-only contracting, the law creates an employer-employee relationship between the principal and the workers. The contractor is merely an agent of the principal employer who is responsible to the workers in the same manner and extent as if the latter were directly employed by the principal.
